questions.question: What is Devise and how does it handle authentication in Rails?
questions.title: Devise Authentication Basics
questions.direct_answer: Devise is a gem that gives you a full authentication system — sign up, login, logout, password reset, confirmable, lockable — from a few generators. You add it to the Gemfile, rails g devise:install, then rails g devise User, which creates a migration (with encrypted_password, reset_password columns) and a User model with the Devise modules, and gives you helpers like current_user, authenticate_user!, and the sign in/out routes. It's built on Warden and gives you a tested, convention-over-configuration auth layer instead of writing login from scratch.

sections.title: A Full Auth System From Generators
sections.content: Devise is a gem that gives you a full authentication system — sign up, login, logout, password reset, confirmable, lockable, trackable — from a few generators. You add it to the Gemfile, run rails g devise:install, then rails g devise User, which creates a migration (with encrypted_password, reset_password_token columns) and a User model with the Devise modules, and gives you controller/view helpers like current_user, authenticate_user!, and user_signed_in?, plus the sign in/out routes. It's built on Warden and gives you a tested, convention-over-configuration auth layer instead of writing login, password hashing, and session management from scratch.

sections.title: From Generator to Working Auth
sections.content:
devise:install sets up the config; g devise User generates the migration, model, routes, and helpers.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  G[gem 'devise'] --> I[devise:install]
  I --> U[g devise User]
  U --> M[migration + model with Devise modules]
  U --> R[devise_for :users routes]
  U --> H[current_user, authenticate_user!]
```

sections.title: Setting up Devise
sections.content:
```ruby
# 1) Gemfile
gem 'devise'
# then: bundle install

# 2) Install
rails g devise:install

# 3) Generate the User model (migration + model + routes)
rails g devise User
# migration adds: encrypted_password, reset_password_token, reset_password_sent_at, ...

# 4) app/models/user.rb
class User < ApplicationRecord
  devise :database_authenticatable, :registerable,
         :recoverable, :rememberable, :validatable
end

# 5) Helpers now available in controllers/views:
current_user              # the signed-in user, or nil
user_signed_in?          # boolean
authenticate_user!        # before_action to require login

# 6) routes.rb (generated by devise_for :users)
new_user_session_path     # login
new_user_registration_path # sign up
destroy_user_session_path # logout
```

sections.title: Common Mistakes
items: Rolling your own auth when Devise is the Rails convention — use Devise.
Not understanding what g devise User generates (migration + model + routes + helpers).
Forgetting to run rails g devise:install before g devise User (config missing).

sections.title: Key Takeaways
items: Devise is a gem giving a full auth system (signup/login/logout/reset) from generators.
rails g devise:install sets up config; rails g devise User creates the model, migration, and routes.
It gives helpers: current_user, user_signed_in?, authenticate_user! (a before_action).
Devise modules (database_authenticatable, registerable, recoverable) toggle features.
It's built on Warden and gives a tested, convention-over-configuration auth layer.

sections.title: Spoken Answer
sections.content: Devise is a gem that gives you a full authentication system — sign up, login, logout, password reset, confirmable, lockable, trackable — from a few generators. You add it to the Gemfile, run rails g devise colon install, then rails g devise User, which creates a migration with the encrypted password and reset password token columns and a User model with the Devise modules, and gives you controller and view helpers like current_user, authenticate_user bang, and user signed in question mark, plus the sign in and sign out routes. It's built on Warden and gives you a tested, convention-over-configuration auth layer instead of writing login, password hashing, and session management from scratch. A common mistake is rolling your own auth when Devise is the Rails convention, and not understanding what g devise User actually generates, which is a migration, a model, routes, and helpers.
